title: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Differences in shape among related animals are largely due to different patterns of relative growth rates of their parts, so their shapes are related by simple smooth geometric transformations.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: differences between the shapes and forms of animals may often be due in large part merely to different patterns in the rates of growth for their different parts.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Growth of Plants and Animals” (from p. 400), p. 421. Scope: body shapes of animals within a family or order

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-24: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public 3D morphology supports direct tests of smooth geometric relatedness across many taxa. Paired developmental growth-rate data are much less complete, limiting mechanistic inference. Existing resources can resolve geometric and selected developmental subsets, not the broad causal statement.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Register three-dimensional shapes of related animals, fit low-dimensional smooth deformation fields, and compare inferred regional scaling with measured developmental growth rates. The claim is supported when simple growth-rate differences predict held-out adult shape differences better than alternatives.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Adult transformations do not uniquely identify developmental growth processes.

Time-resolved growth data are sparse relative to mature morphology.

Largely and simple require variance and complexity thresholds.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.64
data adequacy: 0.52
operationalizability: 0.72
data existence: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Geometric morphometrics is a standard test of whether related forms differ by smooth transformations, and public specimen media cover several well-studied families. A successful warp does not establish relative growth rate as the cause, and many taxa have no landmark series. The claim is testable for shape description in a subset of animals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place landmarks on related species within a family or order and test whether the shape differences are smooth relative warps consistent with different regional growth rates. A low-dimensional smooth transformation relating the shapes would support the claim; discrete additions of parts that no smooth warp removes would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Landmark datasets are dense for some vertebrate groups and absent for most animal orders.

A smooth geometric map can describe a difference that was not produced by altered growth rates.

analysis feasibility: 0.6
